canonicalExplanation.summary: JavaScript has seven **primitive** types — string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol — and everything else is an **object** (arrays, functions, dates…). Primitives are **immutable**: you can read `name[0]`, but you can't change it in place — string methods return **new** strings. `typeof` classifies values (with one historic quirk: `typeof null` is "object"). `undefined` means "not set yet"; `null` means "deliberately empty".

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You try to capitalise a name with `name[0] = "A"`. No error — and nothing changes. Strings look like arrays of letters, but they don't behave like them. Changing one character creates a new string value rather than mutating the existing primitive. In this lesson you'll classify primitive and object values and explain null and undefined use cases.

```predict
{"question": "`let s = \"asha\"; s[0] = \"A\"; console.log(s);` Output?", "options": ["\"Asha\"", "\"asha\""], "answer": 1, "why": "Strings are immutable primitives. The assignment is silently ignored (or throws in strict mode). Build a new string instead."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Scripts and console** and **Expressions and evaluation** — values are what expressions produce.

sections.heading: The distinction: primitives vs objects
sections.body:
| Value | typeof | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| `"hi"`. | "string". | primitive. |
| `42`, `NaN`. | "number". | primitive. |
| `10n`. | "bigint". | primitive. |
| `true`. | "boolean". | primitive. |
| `undefined`. | "undefined". | primitive. |
| `null`. | "object" (historic quirk!). | primitive. |
| `Symbol("id")`. | "symbol". | primitive. |
| `[1, 2]`, `{}`. | "object". | object. |
| `function () {}`. | "function". | object. |

```js
const name = "asha";
const fixed = name[0].toUpperCase() + name.slice(1);  // "Asha" — a NEW string
console.log(name);   // still "asha"
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "How do you check for null correctly?", "answer": "`value === null`. Don't use typeof for null, because it says \"object\". Use `Array.isArray(x)` to detect arrays."}
```

sections.heading: undefined vs null

includes: Classify values as primitives or objects with typeof, === null and Array.isArray.
Explain string immutability and when to use null vs undefined.

outcomes: Classify primitive and object values and explain null and undefined use cases.

examples.title: Changing one letter makes a new string
examples.situation: Changing one character creates a new string value rather than mutating the existing primitive.
walkthrough: **Attempt:** `name[0] = "A"` does nothing — the existing primitive can't be mutated.
**New string:** `const fixed = name[0].toUpperCase() + name.slice(1)` creates a new string value "Asha".
**Check:** `console.log(name, fixed)` will print "asha Asha" — the original is unchanged.
examples.result: The capitalised name is a new string; the original primitive never changed.

examples.title: The null that passed a typeof check
examples.situation: `if (typeof user === "object") { show(user.name); }` crashes with "Cannot read properties of null".
walkthrough: `typeof null` is "object", so the check passes for null.
Fix: `if (user !== null && typeof user === "object")` — or better, `if (user) { … }` when any object is fine.
examples.result: The code handles a deliberately empty user without crashing.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Strings are mutable arrays because bracket access returns characters.
misconceptions.correction: Bracket access only reads characters. Strings are immutable primitives: every change (toUpperCase, slice, replace, +) produces a new string, leaving the original unchanged.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Changing one letter makes a new string", why did name stay "asha"?

analogy.example: A string is like a **printed word on a card**: you can read any letter, but to change one you print a new card. Objects are like **whiteboards** — you can wipe and rewrite parts in place.
limitations: Cards pile up physically; old strings are cleaned up automatically.
null is a blank card you placed on purpose; undefined is no card at all.

steps.explanation: The name holds an immutable string primitive.
Assigning to one character cannot mutate the existing primitive.
Changing one character creates a new string value instead.

trace.textAlternative: Trying to change a string. Step 1, Original: name is 'asha'; typeof name is string. The name holds an immutable string primitive. Step 2, Attempted change: name is 'asha' (unchanged). Assigning to one character cannot mutate the existing primitive. Step 3, New value: fixed is 'Asha'; name is 'asha'. Changing one character creates a new string value instead.

remediation.explanation: To classify: **=== null first → Array.isArray → typeof.** To change a string: always assign the result of a method to a variable.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply the classification order to "The null that passed a typeof check".

recap.summary: To classify primitive and object values, use === null, Array.isArray and typeof (remembering typeof null is "object"). Strings and other primitives are immutable — methods return new values. Use undefined for "not set" and null for a deliberate empty value.
